claim: Malaria poses a significant public health challenge globally, with an estimated 263 million clinical cases and 597,000 deaths occurring in 2023.
source: Malaria is a mosquito-borne disease caused by Plasmodium parasites. It poses a significant public health challenge globally, with an estimated 263 million clinical cases and 597,000 deaths occurring in 2023 (World Health Organization, 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the World Health Organization 2024 report.

claim: Malaria reduction has slowed or plateaued in recent years due to multiple factors including antimalarial drug resistance and lack of highly efficacious vaccines and detailed, timely surveillance.
source: Despite intensive efforts toward malaria control and elimination, malaria reduction has slowed or plateaued in recent years, due to multiple factors including antimalarial drug resistance and lack of highly efficacious vaccines and detailed, timely surveillance.
evidence: The claim is supported by general knowledge about malaria control challenges.

claim: Identity-by-descent (IBD) has been used to estimate genetic relatedness.
source: Identity-by-descent (IBD) is an essential tool in population genomics that has been used to estimate genetic relatedness (Taylor et al., 2019b; Gerlovina et al., 2022; Henden et al., 2018; Schaffner et al., 2023)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Identity-by-descent (IBD) has been used to estimate positive selection.
source: Identity-by-descent (IBD) is an essential tool in population genomics that has been used to estimate genetic relatedness (Taylor et al., 2019b; Gerlovina et al., 2022; Henden et al., 2018; Schaffner et al., 2023), positive selection (Henden et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2024; Browning and Browning, 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Identity-by-descent (IBD) has been used to estimate effective population size (Ne).
source: Identity-by-descent (IBD) is an essential tool in population genomics that has been used to estimate genetic relatedness (Taylor et al., 2019b; Gerlovina et al., 2022; Henden et al., 2018; Schaffner et al., 2023), positive selection (Henden et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2024; Browning and Browning, 2020), effective population size (Ne) (Gutenkunst et al., 2009; Morgan et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Identity-by-descent (IBD) has been used to estimate fine-scale population structure.
source: Identity-by-descent (IBD) is an essential tool in population genomics that has been used to estimate genetic relatedness (Taylor et al., 2019b; Gerlovina et al., 2022; Henden et al., 2018; Schaffner et al., 2023), positive selection (Henden et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2024; Browning and Browning, 2020), effective population size (Ne) (Gutenkunst et al., 2009; Morgan et al., 2020), fine-scale population structure (Guo et al., 2024; Shetty et al., 2019; Nait Saada et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Identity-by-descent (IBD) has been used to estimate migration patterns.
source: Identity-by-descent (IBD) is an essential tool in population genomics that has been used to estimate genetic relatedness (Taylor et al., 2019b; Gerlovina et al., 2022; Henden et al., 2018; Schaffner et al., 2023), positive selection (Henden et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2024; Browning and Browning, 2020), effective population size (Ne) (Gutenkunst et al., 2009; Morgan et al., 2020), fine-scale population structure (Guo et al., 2024; Shetty et al., 2019; Nait Saada et al., 2020), and migration patterns (Shetty et al., 2019; Al-Asadi et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: In high transmission settings, a rapid decrease in genetic diversity and effective population size may indicate a successful malaria intervention.
source: In high transmission settings, a rapid decrease in genetic diversity and effective population size may indicate a successful malaria intervention (Morgan et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Plasmodium falciparum genomes recombine about 70 times more frequently per unit of physical distance than the human genome.
source: More importantly, Pf genomes recombine about 70 times more frequently per unit of physical distance (Gardner et al., 2002; Su et al., 1999; Jiang et al., 2011; Amambua-Ngwa et al., 2019; Miles et al., 2016) than the human genome (Kong et al., 2002)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research comparing recombination rates.

claim: Plasmodium falciparum shares a similar mutation rate as human genomes on the order of 10^-8 per base pair per generation.
source: while sharing a similar mutation rate (Bopp et al., 2013; Camponovo et al., 2023; Churcher et al., 2014; Hamilton et al., 2017; Huber et al., 2016; McDew-White et al., 2019; Neafsey et al., 2021) as human genomes (Campbell et al., 2012) on the order of 10–8 per base pair per generation.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research on mutation rates.

claim: Large human whole-genome sequencing data sets typically provide millions of common biallelic SNP variants.
source: Large human whole-genome sequencing data sets typically provide millions of common biallelic SNP variants (Taliun et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Plasmodium falciparum data sets only have tens of thousands of common biallelic SNP variants.
source: while Pf data sets only have tens of thousands (Abdel Hamid et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The human genome is about twice as large as Plasmodium falciparum in genetic units.
source: Given that the human genome is about twice as large as Pf in genetic units, the per-centimorgan (cM) SNP density in Pf can be two orders of magnitude lower than in humans
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparison of genome sizes and SNP densities.

claim: The per-centimorgan SNP density in Plasmodium falciparum can be two orders of magnitude lower than in humans.
source: Given that the human genome is about twice as large as Pf in genetic units, the per-centimorgan (cM) SNP density in Pf can be two orders of magnitude lower than in humans
evidence: The claim is based on inference from genome size and SNP variant data.

claim: The density of common biallelic SNPs per cM in selectively neutral scenarios is inversely correlated with recombination rates ranging from 3 × 10^-9 to 10^-6 per base pair per generation.
source: Under a single-population demographic model (see Methods), we found that the density of common biallelic SNPs (minor allele frequency ≥ 0.01) per cM, in selectively neutral scenarios, is inversely correlated with recombination rates ranging from 3 × 10–9 to 10–6 per base pair per generation (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from simulations shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The SNP density of Plasmodium falciparum-like genomes is 25 SNPs per cM.
source: For instance, the SNP density of Pf-like genomes is 25 SNPs per cM, which is approximately 1/67 of that of the human-like genomes (1660 SNPs per cM).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: The SNP density of human-like genomes is 1660 SNPs per cM.
source: For instance, the SNP density of Pf-like genomes is 25 SNPs per cM, which is approximately 1/67 of that of the human-like genomes (1660 SNPs per cM).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: As the recombination rate increases, both the genome-wide false negative rate and false positive rate increase for IBD inferred from hmmIBD.
source: Our analysis showed that as the recombination rate increases, both the genome-wide FN and FP (Figure 2b) increase for IBD inferred from hmmIBD.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: All IBD detection methods suffer elevated false negative rates and/or false positive rates as the recombination rate increases, with the exception of isoRelate.
source: The patterns vary in the other four IBD detection methods, and all suffer elevated FNs and/or FPs as the recombination rate increases (Figure 2b; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), with the exception of isoRelate, which has better IBD quality with lower marker densities.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: isoRelate has better IBD quality with lower marker densities.
source: The patterns vary in the other four IBD detection methods, and all suffer elevated FNs and/or FPs as the recombination rate increases (Figure 2b; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), with the exception of isoRelate, which has better IBD quality with lower marker densities.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Low SNP density per genetic unit can dramatically affect the reliability of detected IBD segments.
source: The results suggest that low SNP density per genetic unit can dramatically affect the reliability of detected IBD segments.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the simulation results showing increased error rates with higher recombination rates.

claim: By default, hmmIBD has relatively low false negative and false positive error rates.
source: We found that by default, hmmIBD has relatively low FN/FP error rates (Figure 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: By default, hmmIBD is less biased for relatedness estimates.
source: We found that by default, hmmIBD has relatively low FN/FP error rates (Figure 3) and is less biased for relatedness estimates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: isoRelate and human-oriented callers have high false negative rates and varying false positive rates.
source: In contrast, isoRelate and human-oriented callers have high FN rates and varying FP rates (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The false negative rates of IBD called from hap-IBD change substantially when the min-marker parameter varies.
source: For example, the FN rates of IBD called from hap-IBD change substantially when the min-marker parameter varies (see Supplementary file 2—Data S2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Supplementary file 2—Data S2.

claim: With a min-marker value of 70, the false negative rate for short IBD segments dramatically decreases such that the false negative and false positive error rates become more balanced for hap-IBD.
source: With a value of 70, the FN rate for short IBD segments dramatically decreases such that the FN and FP error rates become more balanced (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Genetic relatedness estimates change from being highly underestimated before parameter optimization to being more balanced after optimization for hap-IBD.
source: Consistently, genetic relatedness estimates change from being highly underestimated before parameter optimization (Figure 4b, left column) to being more balanced after optimization (Figure 4b, right column).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Similar improvements in IBD quality were observed for Refined IBD and phased IBD after parameter optimization.
source: Similar improvements were observed for Refined IBD and phased IBD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The quality metrics remained largely unchanged during parameter optimization attempts for hmmIBD and isoRelate.
source: In contrast, the quality metrics remained largely unchanged during parameter optimization attempts for hmmIBD and isoRelate, with hmmIBD being more accurate and unbiased and isoRelate suffering from high false negative rates and underestimated relatedness (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most callers can capture the majority of the simulated selection signals except Refined IBD, which only detects 2-3 out of 14 selected loci.
source: We found that most callers can capture the majority of the simulated signals except Refined IBD, which is less sensitive and only detects 2–3 out of 14 selected loci (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: isoRelate shows an increased level of false positives or low signal-to-noise ratios in IBD coverage curves for selection detection.
source: isoRelate shows an increased level of false positives or low signal-to-noise ratios, evident in IBD coverage curves (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: IBD inferred from most callers can accurately recapitulate the simulated population structure, comparable to true IBD.
source: Similarly to IBD-based selection signal detection, we found that IBD inferred from most callers can accurately recapitulate the simulated population structure, comparable to true IBD (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: isoRelate tends to generate many smaller groups in population structure inference, likely due to high false negative rates for short IBD segments.
source: The exception is that isoRelate tends to generate many smaller groups, which is likely due to high FN rates for short IBD segments, missing connectivity among distantly related genomes, and only showing closely related subgroups of small sizes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed pattern and known characteristics of isoRelate.

claim: Most of the compared IBD callers suffer from wild oscillations in Ne estimates and deviate significantly from the truth for older generations.
source: We found most of the compared IBD callers suffer from wild oscillations, which have previously been observed (Browning and Browning, 2015), and deviate significantly from the truth for older generations (Figure 5)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5 and a citation to previous observations.

claim: The IBD inferred by hmmIBD generated highly accurate Ne estimates comparable to true IBD.
source: Meanwhile, the IBD inferred by hmmIBD generated highly accurate estimates comparable to true IBD (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The strong bias in Ne estimates is likely due to the underestimation of population-level total IBD for short IBD segments.
source: We explored the mechanisms underlying bias in Ne estimates and found that the strong bias is likely due to the underestimation of population-level total IBD for short IBD segments, which is most obvious for hap-IBD, isoRelate, and phased IBD, followed by Refined IBD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: For hmmIBD, both the estimates of Ne and population total IBD are relatively unbiased.
source: For hmmIBD, both the estimates of Ne (Figure 5) and population total IBD are relatively unbiased (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, column 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: IBD-based Ne estimates are highly sensitive to the quality of input IBD segments.
source: These results suggest that IBD-based Ne estimates are highly sensitive to the quality of input IBD segments, and that hmmIBD is more accurate for this analysis.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed differences in Ne estimation accuracy across different IBD callers.

claim: hmmIBD is more accurate for Ne estimation analysis.
source: These results suggest that IBD-based Ne estimates are highly sensitive to the quality of input IBD segments, and that hmmIBD is more accurate for this analysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing hmmIBD's superior performance in Ne estimation.

claim: Removing IBD segments with TMRCA < 1.5 generations can greatly mitigate the oscillation problem in Ne estimates, especially for hmmIBD and Refined IBD.
source: We found that removing these segments can greatly mitigate this problem (Figure 5—figure supplement 3a), especially for hmmIBD and Refined IBD.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3a.

claim: All callers, except Refined IBD, capture most known selection signals from the Southeast Asia data set with optimized parameters.
source: With optimized parameters, all callers, except Refined IBD, capture most known selection signals from the Southeast Asia data set.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from empirical analysis of the Southeast Asia data set.

claim: Known selection signals in the Southeast Asia data set include selective sweeps associated with antimalarial drug resistance and sexual commitment, such as dhfr, pfmdr1, pfaat1, pfcrt, dhps, ap2-g and arps10.
source: These signals include selective sweeps associated with antimalarial drug resistance and sexual commitment, such as dihydrofolate reductase (dhfr) (Miotto et al., 2013), multidrug resistance protein 1 (pfmdr1) (Koenderink et al., 2010), amino acid transporter 1 (pfaat1) (Amambua-Ngwa et al., 2019), chloroquine resistance transporter (pfcrt) (Martin and Kirk, 2004), dihydropteroate synthase (dhps) (Brooks et al., 1994), Apicomplexan-specific ApiAP2-g (ap2-g) (Early et al., 2022) and apicoplast ribosomal protein S10 (arps10) (Miotto et al., 2015; Figure 6a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research and data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: hmmIBD detects more peaks but suffers from noise in selection signal detection, likely due to the relatively high false positive to false negative ratios for short (<4 cM) IBD segments.
source: hmmIBD detects more peaks but suffers from noise, likely due to the relatively high FP to FN ratios for short (<4 cM) IBD segments (Figure 2 and Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3.

claim: IBD detected using most callers resulted in Ne estimates with unrealistic oscillations for the Southeast Asia data set, including extremely large estimates in the more distant past (> 20 generations ago).
source: Similar to the simulation analysis, IBD detected using most callers resulted in Ne estimates with unrealistic oscillations for the Southeast Asia data set, including extremely large estimates in the more distant past (> 20 generations ago; Figure 6b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The Ne estimation problems are much less severe with the estimates from hmmIBD, which mirrored the expected reduction in malaria in Southeast Asia due to intense efforts to eliminate malaria in recent decades.
source: The problems are much less severe with the estimates from hmmIBD, which mirrored the expected reduction in malaria in this region due to the intense efforts to eliminate malaria in recent decades (World Health Organization, 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from empirical analysis and a citation to WHO report.

claim: InfoMap-based community detection reveals expected continental population structure across most callers: African Plasmodium falciparum parasites are less structured, and Southeast Asian parasites are more structured and distinct from Oceanian parasites.
source: InfoMap-based community detection reveals expected continental population structure across most callers: African Pf parasites are less structured, and Southeast Asian parasites are more structured and distinct from Oceanian parasites (Figure 6c), consistent with previous non-IBD-based methods (Abdel Hamid et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6c and a citation to previous research.

claim: isoRelate IBD estimates generate many small, close groups in population structure inference, likely due to high false negative rates for short IBD segments, especially in high transmission settings like Africa.
source: isoRelate IBD estimates generate many small, close groups, likely due to high false negative rates for short IBD segments, especially in high transmission settings like Africa where parasites have low relatedness and mainly share short IBD segments (Figure 6c).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from data shown in Figure 6c and known characteristics of isoRelate.

claim: When using a single thread, probabilistic inference algorithms like isoRelate, Refined IBD, and hmmIBD are about two orders of magnitude slower than those based on identity-by-state-based or positional Burrows-Wheeler transform (PBWT) based algorithms, such as hap-IBD and phased IBD.
source: When using a single thread, probabilistic inference algorithms like isoRelate, Refined IBD, and hmmIBD are about two orders of magnitude slower than those based on identity-by-state-based or positional Burrows-Wheeler transform (PBWT) based algorithms, such as hap-IBD and phased IBD (Figure 7a).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Maximum memory consumption is highest in Refined IBD, with hmmIBD being around 10 times more efficient.
source: Maximum memory consumption is highest in Refined IBD, with hmmIBD being around 10 times more efficient (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: hmmIBD currently only supports single-thread computation.
source: The exception is hmmIBD, as it currently only supports single-thread computation.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of hmmIBD's implementation.

claim: Low marker density per genetic distance significantly affects IBD detection accuracy.
source: Our findings indicate that low marker density per genetic distance significantly affects IBD detection accuracy.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the simulation and empirical results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Optimizing parameters of IBD detection methods for Plasmodium genomes enhances the accuracy of detected IBD segments.
source: Optimizing parameters of IBD detection methods for Plasmodium genomes enhances the accuracy of detected IBD segments, thereby improving subsequent downstream analyses such as the inference of positive selection signals and population structures.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing improved performance after parameter optimization.

claim: We generally recommend hmmIBD for IBD estimation in Plasmodium genomes when phased genotype data of haploid genomes are available.
source: We generally recommend hmmIBD for IBD estimation in Plasmodium genomes when phased genotype data of haploid genomes are available.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comprehensive benchmarking results showing hmmIBD's superior performance.

claim: The effective population size of humans has increased rapidly in recent history.
source: The effective population size of humans has increased rapidly in recent history (Gutenkunst et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The effective population size of Plasmodium falciparum is decreasing, particularly in regions such as Southeast Asia and South America, due to enhanced malaria elimination efforts.
source: while that of Pf is decreasing, particularly in regions such as Southeast Asia and South America (Joy et al., 2003; World Health Organization, 2024), due to enhanced malaria elimination efforts.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The recombination rate of Plasmodium falciparum is 6.67 × 10^-7 per base pair per generation.
source: In these simulations, we assumed constant recombination rates over the genome, such as 6.67 × 10–7 per base pair per generation for Pf (Amambua-Ngwa et al., 2019; Conway et al., 1999)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The recombination rate of humans is 1.0 × 10^-8 per base pair per generation.
source: and 1.0 × 10–8 for humans (Kong et al., 2002)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The mutation rate is 1.0 × 10^-8 per base pair per generation for both Plasmodium falciparum and humans.
source: and a mutation rate of 1.0 × 10–8 for both Pf (Camponovo et al., 2023; Bopp et al., 2013) and humans unless otherwise specified.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.
